title: Handle the Morning the Feed Breaks
scenario: The feed contract you profiled at Easy tier just got violated twice in one morning: the file is late, and when it finally lands, one row is malformed. The brief still ships at 7:00. Your job is to execute the runbook and produce the incident record that proves the failure was handled, not hidden.
input:
Timeline:
- 6:15 AM: feed expected. Nothing arrives.
- 6:20 AM: workflow detects the feed is late and opens an incident.
- 6:42 AM: feed arrives. The SPP row is malformed - its settled column reads 'n/a'.

Runbook for feed incidents:
1. Log the incident with expected and actual arrival times.
2. Malformed rows are QUARANTINED - held aside untouched for the vendor to inspect. Never dropped silently, never guessed.
3. The brief proceeds in DEGRADED mode and must say so - readers deserve to know today's numbers are partial.
4. Notify the Risk Desk Lead (owner of upstream data quality).
instructions: Work through the runbook in order - each numbered step maps to fields in the record.
Record the timing facts: expected, detected, arrived.
Record what was wrong, what was done with the bad row, and the brief's mode.
Return one JSON object - the incident record - then validate.
copilotPrompt: Write a feed-incident record as JSON with incidentType, expectedAt, detectedAt, arrivedAt, malformedRowHub, malformedRowAction, briefMode, and notified, following this runbook: quarantine malformed rows, run the brief in degraded mode, notify the data-quality owner.
successMessage: Incident handled and recorded. The workflow failed gracefully, visibly, and on schedule - which is what resilience actually means.

intro.heading: Before you build: failure is a mode, not a surprise

sections.title: Contracts break; runbooks answer
sections.body: At Easy tier you read the feed's contract. Hard tier is the morning the contract is violated. Mature automation does not prevent every failure - it decides IN ADVANCE what each failure means and what happens next. That decision, written down, is a runbook.

sections.title: Quarantine beats both alternatives
sections.body: Drop the SPP row silently and nobody learns the vendor has a problem. Guess its value and the brief lies. Quarantine - hold the row untouched, visibly - preserves both the evidence and the truth.

sections.title: Degraded mode is honest shipping
sections.body: The brief ships at 7:00 with partial data AND SAYS SO. Readers who know the numbers are partial can act accordingly; readers who are not told cannot. Silent degradation is the failure mode that destroys trust in automation.

sections.title: Detection is its own timestamp
sections.body: The feed was due at 6:15; the workflow NOTICED at 6:20. That five-minute gap is a measurable property of your monitoring - which is why detectedAt is its own field, distinct from expectedAt.

fieldGuide.meaning: What kind of failure this was.
When the contract said the feed arrives.

fieldGuide.hint: Distinct from expected - the gap measures your monitoring.

fieldGuide.meaning: What the runbook does with bad rows.

fieldGuide.hint: Partial data, and it says so.
The owner of upstream data quality.

takeaway.heading: Graceful failure, on the record
points: You executed a failure path that was designed before the failure happened - the defining trait of resilient automation.
The bad row is quarantined evidence, not a silent gap or a plausible lie.
The brief ships degraded and says so: honest partial output beats punctual fiction.
The incident record captures detection lag, actions, and notification - everything a postmortem needs, written while it happened.
The workflow can now break visibly and recover gracefully instead of failing silently.
